summary: I reviewed the dvpwa (aiohttp) Python web application: the DAO layer (students, courses, reviews, users, marks), request handlers (views.py), routing, auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 setup and templates, session/DB/Redis services, and config. Overall risk is critical: the app exposes an unauthenticated SQL injection that grants full database access, compounded by disabled HTML auto-escaping (stored XSS), disabled CSRF protection, JS-readable session cookies, unsalted MD5 password hashing, and missing authorization on state-changing endpoints. These are largely intentional (it is a deliberately vulnerable app), but all are real and reachable. Coverage was the entire Python source tree and templates; I did not run or build anything.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via unsanitized string formatting
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the caller-supplied name directly into the SQL string instead of using a parameterized query. The name comes straight from untrusted POST data: views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) reads data['name'] from request.post() and passes it to Student.create. The /students/ POST route (sqli/routes.py:14) has no authorization decorator, so an unauthenticated remote attacker can reach it. Because psycopg/aiopg execute allows multiple statements, an attacker can break out of the single-quoted VALUES('%(name)s') context and run stacked queries, giving full read/write access to the database (dumping users/pwd_hash, altering marks, etc.). This is the representative instance; other DAO methods correctly use parameter binding, so this is the only injectable sink.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  # name = data['name'] from POST /students/. Payload e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE marks; -- executes as separate statement.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query like the other DAOs: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables render as raw HTML unless a template adds an explicit | e filter (almost none do). User-controlled data is stored and later rendered unescaped: course review text (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 renders review.review_text), student names (sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16), and course title/description (course.jinja2:14-15). Review creation (POST /courses/{id}/review, sqli/views.py:129) and student creation are reachable without authentication, so an attacker can persist a <script> payload that executes in every visitor's browser when they view the course/student page. Combined with the JS-readable session cookie, this enables session hijacking. Root cause is the global autoescape=False setting.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: course.jinja2 line 22 `{{ review.review_text }}` with review_text from attacker POST.
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the aiohttp_jinja2/Jinja2 default) and use |safe only where HTML output is intentional and trusted.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled for all state-changing POST endpoints
findings.description: A working csrf_middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and validates a per-session _csrf_token on POST, but it is commented out of the middleware list in app.py, so it never runs. Templates emit _csrf_token hidden fields, yet no handler verifies them. As a result every POST action (login, create student, create course, submit review, evaluate/mark a student, logout) accepts cross-site forged requests. An attacker page can silently cause a logged-in admin's browser to create/evaluate records or trigger the SQL-injectable student creation.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware factory that pops/compares session['_csrf_token'] against formdata is defined but unused.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain (and ensure it runs after session_middleware) so the token comparison in middlewares.py:28-37 is enforced on all POSTs.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (student/course/mark/review creation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students and is intended for admins only (the UI form is gated behind auth_user.is_admin in course.jinja2:41), but the handler and its route (sqli/routes.py:21-23) carry no @authorize decorator, so any unauthenticated user can POST grades. The same missing-authorization pattern applies to student creation (views.py:52-60 / routes.py:14) and course creation (views.py:83-93 / routes.py:17-18), which the UI only shows to logged-in users. The authorize() decorator exists (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) but is applied only to logout. This lets anonymous users tamper with grades and create arbitrary records. evaluate is the representative sink because it is clearly admin-only by design.
findings.evidence: @template('evaluate.jinja2') async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) — no @authorize(ensure_admin=True); route added with no auth wrapper in routes.py:21-23.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() to student/course creation handlers (or wrap the routes), matching the access model implied by the templates.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing/verification
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored pwd_hash against md5(password) with no salt and a fast, cryptographically broken hash. Password hashes (retrievable via the SQL injection above, or a DB breach) are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/brute force, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. This weakens credential confidentiality for all accounts.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hashing function such as bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 (e.g. passlib or hashlib.scrypt) and migrate stored hashes; also use a constant-time comparison.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis-backed session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is exposed to client-side JavaScript. Given the disabled autoescaping and resulting stored XSS, an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, enabling account/session hijacking. There is no reason for the app's own JS to read the session cookie.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is True) and additionally set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.
